title: Floating Saunas: What It’s Like to Sauna on the Water in Pemberton
excerpt: Wood-fired saunas on the water, then a plunge into a forest swimming hole: what a session at Pemberton’s floating sauna involves, what the claims get right, and how to do the cold part safely.
short_answer: A floating sauna is a wood-fired sauna built on a pontoon, so you step straight from the heat into open water. Western Australia’s first opened in 2026 on Pemberton Pool, a karri-forest swimming hole about 3.5 hours from Perth. Sessions run an hour: $55 a person shared, or $305 for a private sauna. The heat is well studied; the cold plunge needs more care than the videos suggest.
what_it_is:
A floating sauna is what it sounds like: a sauna room built on a floating platform, moored on a lake or river. You warm up inside, then leave by the door and get into the water instead of a shower or a tiled plunge pool. The idea comes from the Nordic countries, and it has reached Australia over the past few years — the first here opened at Derby, Tasmania, in 2020, followed by one on Lake Burley Griffin in Canberra (Broadsheet).

Pemberton Floating Sauna is the same operator’s third site. It sits on Pemberton Pool, a long-standing swimming hole in the karri forest of WA’s Southern Forests and Valleys, about 3.5 hours from Perth and 1.5 hours from Margaret River. There are two independent wood-fired sauna rooms built from imported Finnish cedar, each with a floor-to-ceiling window over the water and forest, and a ladder back up onto the platform from the pool (Floating Sauna; Broadsheet).
why_trending:
Floating saunas film beautifully — steam, tall trees, a leap into still water — and Pemberton’s opened in the winter of 2026 to a wave of posts from travel and tourism accounts, including the Reel on this page. It also sits where two bigger trends meet: social, bathhouse-style saunas, and cold-water plunging.

Posts about both tend to promise a lot — detoxing, immunity, “resetting” the nervous system. This page keeps the experience and the evidence apart.
what_to_expect:
You book a one-hour slot online. A shared session puts you in one of the two saunas with up to six people; a private session gives your group a sauna room to yourselves, with a “Sauna Master” on hand to walk you through the hot and cold rounds (bookings). Most people alternate: time in the heat, a short dip in the pool, a rest, and round again.

The site is off-grid. There are no toilets on the platform — the nearest is about a ten-minute walk — so bring your own towel, drinking water and a change of clothes. There is a car park near the entrance (operator FAQ). It opens 7am to 9pm every day except Christmas Day (Floating Sauna).
reel_context:
What it gets right: the ritual really is that simple — heat, cold water, rest, repeat — and the setting is as calm as it looks.

What needs context: the Reel describes diving straight in. Pemberton Pool is natural water, and Royal Life Saving’s advice for rivers, lakes and dams is to check the depth and not to jump or dive in (Royal Life Saving). Get in feet first or by the ladder unless staff show you exactly where it is deep enough.

The “regret it for three seconds” moment is the cold-shock response: sudden immersion in water below about 15°C can bring an involuntary gasp — which can mean breathing in water — fast breathing and extra strain on the heart (Royal Life Saving WA). That is why a first dip should be short, calm and never alone.

The operator’s founder has described the hot–cold contrast as forcing “a rebalance of chemicals in the nervous system” (Broadsheet). It is a fair description of how it can feel; it is not something research has shown.
possible_benefits:
For most people the draw is simply the experience: warmth, quiet, a forest outside the window, and time with the people you came with.

Sauna bathing itself is one of the better-studied wellness habits. A Finnish study that followed 2,315 middle-aged men for around 20 years found that those who used a sauna more often had lower rates of fatal heart disease (Laukkanen et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015). It was an observational study, so it shows an association rather than proof that saunas caused the difference — and the men were using saunas several times a week for decades.

A 2018 systematic review of 40 studies concluded that regular dry sauna bathing has potential health benefits, while noting most studies were small and that better-quality research is needed (Hussain & Cohen, 2018).
limitations_uncertainties:
“Detox.” Sweat is mostly water and salts. One published estimate found the pollutants the body stores are lost in sweat in negligible amounts, far less than we take in through food (Imbeault et al., Environment International, 2018). We found no good evidence that a sauna detoxes the body.

The cold plunge. A major review of cold-water immersion found the evidence behind its many claimed benefits varies widely: some have a credible rationale, while others remain “at the level of anecdotal speculation” (Tipton et al., Experimental Physiology, 2017).

One visit is not a habit. The sauna research above looks at regular use over years. A single session on a trip away is a lovely experience, not a treatment.
safety_considerations:
Heat and cold both put a real load on the heart and circulation. Drinking alcohol during sauna bathing raises the risk of low blood pressure, heart-rhythm problems and sudden death, and should be avoided; a sauna is also not advised for people with unstable angina, a recent heart attack or severe aortic stenosis (Hannuksela & Ellahham, American Journal of Medicine, 2001).

The cold water is the bigger risk here. Royal Life Saving, AUSactive and SPASA note that cold-water immersion carries an inherent drowning risk, and list shock responses, gasping, cramps, hypothermia and panic among its hazards. They advise building up gradually from short exposures, learning to control your breathing, keeping your head and neck out of the water in plunge settings, and having supervision (Royal Life Saving position statement, 2024). Because Pemberton Pool is natural water, check the depth and don’t dive (Royal Life Saving).
who_may_need_professional_advice:
Talk to your GP, midwife or specialist before you book if you:

  • are pregnant — the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists advises against saunas and hot tubs early in pregnancy because of the rise in core body temperature (ACOG), and Royal Life Saving lists pregnancy among the higher risks for cold immersion;
  • have a heart condition, high blood pressure or circulation problems;
  • take medication, or are on a treatment program, that affects your heart, blood pressure or temperature;
  • have Raynaud’s or are unusually sensitive to cold;
  • have any chronic or serious illness (Royal Life Saving).

The operator itself advises anyone with an existing medical condition to check with their medical practitioner before booking (operator FAQ).
beginner_tips: For a first time, consider a private session: a Sauna Master is on hand to walk you through the hot and cold rounds.
Keep your first spells in the heat short, and get out as soon as you feel dizzy, sick or too hot.
Get into the pool feet first or by the ladder — don’t copy the dive unless staff tell you where it is deep enough.
Keep your head above water, make the first dip brief, and slow your breathing through the first gasp.
Never plunge alone, and skip alcohol before and during your session.
Bring a towel, drinking water and warm dry clothes; it’s off-grid, with no toilets on the platform.
Allow for the drive: about 3.5 hours from Perth, or 1.5 hours from Margaret River.
questions_to_ask_provider: Where is the safest place to get into the pool, and how deep is it there?
Is a staff member on hand during shared sessions, or only for private bookings?
Roughly how cold is the water at the moment?
Are there age limits, and can children come?
What happens to my booking if the weather turns?
Can the platform and saunas be reached if I have limited mobility?
oria_verdict: Worth the drive for the setting alone: a wood-fired sauna in karri forest with a swimming hole outside the door. Treat it as a restorative ritual rather than a treatment, take the cold part slowly — feet first, head above water, never alone — and if you’re pregnant or have a heart condition, talk to your doctor before you book.
typical_duration: 1 hour, alternating heat, a dip and rest
price_notes: $55 per person for a shared session (up to six people per sauna); $305 for a private session for your group, with a Sauna Master on hand. From the operator’s booking page, checked 18 September 2026.
